title: Practical Tech Skills: Networks, Code and Staying Safe
summary: Three job-ready skills, learned by doing: work out subnets like a network technician, write and test your first JavaScript function, and catch phishing emails before they catch you. Each topic has a short reading, a hands-on lab and a quiz.
outcomes: Find the network address, broadcast address and size of an IPv4 subnet, and tell whether two devices share it
Write a JavaScript function with if / else if decisions and test it, including the boundary values
Recognise phishing messages and respond to them safely
prerequisites: Comfortable using a computer or smartphone. No previous programming or networking experience is needed.

lessons.title: Lab: work out the subnet
lessons.intro: Use the binary view to find the network and broadcast addresses. Keep a pen and paper handy.

questions.prompt: How many usable host addresses does a /27 network have?
What is the network address of 192.168.1.130/25?
questions.explanation: /25 splits the last octet at 128. 130 is in the block 128–255, so the network is 192.168.1.128.

questions.prompt: Which subnet mask is the same as /24?
questions.explanation: 24 bits of ones: three full octets of 255.

questions.prompt: Are 10.0.0.14/28 and 10.0.0.17/28 on the same network?
questions.explanation: /28 blocks are 16 addresses: 0–15 and 16–31. 14 and 17 fall in different blocks.

lessons.title: Lab: scores into grades
lessons.intro: Write the function, run the examples, then check it on fresh scores. Your code runs only in your browser.

lessons.title: Functions quiz
lessons.intro: Three questions on functions and conditions.

questions.prompt: What does this return for 70?  if (s > 70) return "A"; else return "B";
questions.explanation: 70 > 70 is false, so the else branch runs. To include 70 use >=.

questions.prompt: What does the return keyword do?
options: Sends a value back and ends the function
Prints a value on the screen
questions.explanation: return ends the function immediately and gives its value to whoever called it.

questions.prompt: Why should you test scores like 39, 40, 44 and 45?
options: They are the most common scores
Mistakes are most likely at the boundaries between grades
questions.explanation: A wrong operator such as > instead of >= only shows up on the boundary value.

lessons.title: Lab: sort the inbox
lessons.intro: Open every email, check who sent it and where its link goes, then mark it safe or phishing.

questions.prompt: An SMS from "your bank" asks for the one-time code you just received. What should you do?
options: Forward it to a friend to check
Never share it; call the bank on its official number
questions.explanation: One-time codes let someone take over your account. Banks never ask for them.

questions.prompt: Which sender address is most likely genuine for Jumia?
questions.explanation: Genuine messages come from the company's own domain.

questions.prompt: What is the safest way to check a link in an email that looks real?
options: Click it quickly and close the page
Reply and ask if it is real
Type the website address yourself instead of clicking
questions.explanation: Going to the site yourself avoids look-alike addresses entirely.

questions.prompt: You clicked a phishing link and typed your school password. What first?
options: Change the password on the real site and report it
Delete the email and forget it
questions.explanation: Acting quickly limits the damage: change the password, then tell the ICT unit.
